title: Can slowing down sound make the world quieter?
blurb: Low, rumbling noise is hard to cancel. Mathematicians designed a 3D-printed material that halves the speed of sound, so a noise canceller can be half the size.

source.name: Frontiers for Young Minds
source.title: Tackling Noise Pollution With Slow Sound

original.title: Deepening subwavelength acoustic resonance via metamaterials with universal broadband elliptical microstructure
original.authors: W. D. Rowley, W. J. Parnell, I. D. Abrahams, S. R. Voisey, J. Lamb, N. Etaix

cards.b: Engines and fans make noise that can harm our health. Sound travels as waves, and one way to cancel noise is a side pipe cut to the right length. But low, rumbling sounds have very long waves, as long as 17 metres. A pipe made for them would be huge. Could a much smaller pipe do the same job?

William Parnell is a professor of applied mathematics at the University of Manchester in England. William Rowley did his PhD in that group, on designing materials that change how we hear sounds. They published this work with colleagues in 2018. Naomi Curati, who shares the group's science with the public, helped write it for kids.

A side pipe called a quarter-wavelength resonator works like this. Sound goes in, bounces back, and meets the incoming sound out of step, so the two cancel. The pipe must be one quarter as long as the sound wave. To get around this, the team used maths to design a metamaterial, a material whose shape gives it unusual powers. They 3D-printed 4 cm side pipes with thin ovals stacked inside, and tested them.

img.alt: Three drawings of a pipe: sound travels along, some goes into a side branch, and the reflected sound cancels the rest
img.credit: Figure 2, Parnell, Rowley and Curati, Frontiers for Young Minds, CC BY 4.0

cards.b: The ovals made sound travel at about half its normal speed, so the waves inside were shorter. A normal 4 cm pipe cancelled sound at 2,000 hertz. Hertz counts waves per second, and fewer means a lower pitch. The metamaterial pipes, the same length, cancelled sound at 1,000 hertz. The best one cut the noise by 5 decibels, a measure of loudness. That is like moving from 100 metres away to 180 metres away.

img.alt: Photos of the three 3D-printed side pipes and a graph of how much each one reduced sound at different pitches
img.credit: Figure 3, Parnell, Rowley and Curati, Frontiers for Young Minds, CC BY 4.0

cards.b: Both metamaterial pipes did exactly what the maths predicted, which is a good sign. But these were small lab tests. The best new pipe cut its sound by 5 decibels. The normal pipe cut its own sound by about 10. Making real parts for engines and fans is still to come.

Noise is more than annoying. In Europe, aircraft noise has harmed the learning of about 12,500 schoolchildren. Noise also leads to around 12,000 early deaths there each year, from stress-related heart disease. Smaller noise cancellers save space and material, and can reach lower, rumbling sounds.

Watch waves add and cancel. Fill a wide steel thali with water and let it go still. Tap the water gently with one finger, while another person taps from the opposite side at the same time. Ripples spread out and meet. In some places the bumps grow bigger. In other places they flatten out. Sound waves add and cancel in the same way, and the side pipe uses this to cancel noise.
Some sounds we love, like birdsong and music. Some we don't, like traffic and drills. If you could switch off one sound in your street forever, which would you choose? Would anyone else miss it?

words.m: the length of one sound wave, from one bump to the next
how many waves pass each second, measured in hertz; high frequency means a high pitch
a unit for how loud a sound is
what happens when two waves meet: they can add up or cancel out
a material whose special shape gives it powers ordinary materials don't have
